Differential endothelial cell remodeling in Down syndrome and APP duplication drives distinct blood brain barrier dysfunction
summary: An extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene (APP) is present in Down syndrome (DS) and APP duplication (APPdup), increasing the risk of Alzheimer disease (AD) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). However, we reported greater vascular A{beta} deposition in APPdup than in DS with AD, suggesting that other triplicated chromosome 21 genes may mitigate CAA severity. We investigated endothelial cell (EC) function and blood brain barrier (BBB) integrity in DS and APPdup using human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived ECs (iECs), assessing their morphology, junctional proteins, A{beta} peptide secretion, barrier function, and transcriptomic profiles. Both DS and APPdup iECs secreted more A{beta}40 A{beta}42 compared with their respective isogenic controls but exhibited distinct A{beta} peptide profiles. DS iECs showed increased junctional protein expression and reduced permeability, whereas APPdup iECs displayed increased permeability. Transcriptomic analysis revealed extensive dysregulation in DS iECs, with enrichment of junctional, adhesion, angiogenic, immune, and apoptosis pathways, and reduced cell-cycle, proliferative, and membrane-targeting signatures. APPdup iECs showed milder changes, including impaired protein targeting and reduced adhesion-related pathways. Despite comparable APP dosage, DS iECs maintained greater junctional integrity and lower permeability than APPdup iECs, potentially contributing to differential CAA vulnerability. However, impaired proliferation and altered angiogenesis may reduce BBB resilience during ageing.

title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance
summary: Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and \textit{k}-means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8--22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC). SC networks derived from deformation-based morphometry (DBM) were evaluated against three complementary biological benchmarks: age-related individual differences, fractional-anisotropy (FA)-based microstructural connectivity of regionally-specific thalamocortical connections, and Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression. Each algorithm demonstrated underlying sensitivity to differing aspects of neurobiology: PCA and OPNMF showed the strongest associations between participant-level component weights and age. NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means showed greater spatial overlap between positive cortical SC and tractography-derived projections. ICA and PCA showed stronger correspondence between thalamic and cortical gene-expression profiles across the transcriptome, whereas NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means more often identified thalamic components with relatively high core-matrix gene expression. This study emphasizes that algorithmic constraints effectively act as biological priors and decomposition methods do not provide neutral compression of the data. We conclude that it is critical to consider whether the algorithmic objective matches the representational geometry of the neurobiology being studied. Overall, our findings suggest that SC studies should select and justify algorithms according to the biological question, explicitly considering whether their constraints favour distributed gradients, overlapping regional parts, or discrete clusters. Meanwhile, interpretations of SC findings could also be informed by the specific algorithmic constraints used to derive them.

title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease
summary: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

title: Brain representations of visual short-term memories during healthy human aging: occipital decline and frontoparietal compensation
summary: Visual short-term memory declines steeply with age, but the link to neural representations of memory content remains unknown. We used fMRI decoding to relate remembered motion-direction representations in visual and frontoparietal cortex to age and performance, in 115 adults, aged 25-87, from the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) cohort. Decoding was strongest in visual cortex, but also significant in frontoparietal regions, with different profiles. Visual representations weakened with memory load and age, and statistically mediated age-related performance decline, especially during recall. This coupling, however, weakened with age: some older adults retained stronger visual representations than performance implied, suggesting impaired access to a partially preserved memory trace. Frontoparietal representations, instead, were largely insensitive to load and strengthened with age during maintenance, partially offsetting performance decline. Therefore, interventions to boost VSTM in older adults might target compensatory frontoparietal representations during memory maintenance, and readout of untapped visual representations at recall.

title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila
summary: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.

title: Lipid Changes due to Low O-GlcNAc and the Downstream Consequences
summary: O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential mammalian glycosyltransferase that installs O-GlcNAc onto thousands of cytosolic and nuclear proteins. Dysregulated glycosylation by OGT is associated with disease states, including cancer and neurodegeneration. However, cellular consequences of acute loss of O-GlcNAc remain poorly understood. Here, we employed a cell-permeable small molecule inhibitor of OGT, OSMI-4, coupled with transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses to characterize the effects of O-GlcNAc depletion in human cell lines. Loss of O-GlcNAc led to changes in expression of lipid metabolism genes and remodeling of the lipidome, with unsaturated phosphatidylcholines (PCs), saturated lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and unsaturated storage lipids accumulating. We also observed increased lipid droplets. Our results suggest that polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) accumulate in the membrane under low O-GlcNAc conditions and that cells buffer this accumulation by removing PUFAs from membrane lipids and sequestering them in lipid droplets. We found that treatment with OSMI-4 sensitizes cells to ferroptosis inducers, likely because accumulated cell membrane PUFAs undergo peroxidation. Taken together, our results highlight lipid remodeling as an important process that mediates the downstream effects of loss of O-GlcNAc. It may be possible to exploit the synergy between OGT inhibitors and ferroptosis inducers for therapeutic benefit.

title: iPSC modeling of pulmonary arterial hypertension to uncover pathomechanisms and unrecognized modes of action of sotatercept
summary: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a potentially fatal disease characterized by obliterative remodeling of distal pulmonary arteries, commonly associated with bone morphogenetic receptor type 2 (BMPR2) gene mutations. In patients with PAH, sotatercept, an activin signaling inhibitor, improves hemodynamics and outcomes, but clinical responses vary ranging from rapid improvements within weeks to no clinical benefit, suggesting additional mechanisms beyond its anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects. Using patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived smooth muscle cells (iSMCs) with BMPR2 extracellular- or kinase-domain mutations, we reproduced Activin A-driven PAH traits, including hyperproliferation, reduced apoptosis, enhanced contraction and excessive matrix production. We identified smooth muscle cell-to-myofibroblast transition as a previously unknown contributor to pulmonary vascular remodeling and demonstrated its inhibition by sotatercept. Beyond its established effects, sotatercept rapidly reduced contractility, collagen-integrin mechanotransduction and TGFbeta receptor expression, disrupting a pathological positive feedback loop, reflected by lower levels of circulating TGFbeta1 in patients on sotatercept. Taken together, our patient-derived iSMC platform links mutation-dependent mechanisms of pulmonary vascular remodeling to variable drug responsiveness and reveals previously unrecognized, potentially rapid-acting modes of sotatercept in PAH.

title: mTOR signalling, not clock gene rhythms, organises daily physiology
summary: Daily rhythms in mammalian physiology are widely attributed to rhythmic transcription of "clock-controlled genes" driven by the circadian transcriptional/translational feedback loop (TTFL). Here we show that daily physiology can be uncoupled from the TTFL: inhibiting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) abolishes most daily variation in cellular and organismal physiology, whilst clock protein rhythms persist. In cultured cells and mouse liver, functional rhythms are lost, including the proteome, RNA abundance, substrate utilisation and drug metabolism. In forebrain, most daily variation in protein abundance and phosphorylation is lost, yet locomotor activity and sleep-wake architecture are largely preserved in mice and zebrafish. PERIOD2 binds mTORC1 and limits its activity, providing a route by which clock proteins shape daily mTOR signalling. mTOR inhibition preferentially suppresses output over clock gene rhythms in Arabidopsis and Neurospora. We conclude that mTOR is a conserved conduit through which circadian and environmental timing impose daily organisation on physiology.

title: Knockdown of the long non-coding RNA DNAAF3-AS1 activates the p53 pathway and remodels the H3K36me3 landscape
summary: Long non-coding RNAs are increasingly recognised as chromatin regulators, yet most remain functionally uncharacterised. DNAAF3-AS1, transcribed antisense to the ciliary dynein assembly factor gene DNAAF3, is almost exclusively associated with H3K36me3 in the HiMoRNA database. H3K36me3 ChIP-seq in human dermal fibroblasts following DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown with two independent antisense oligonucleotides revealed a marked reduction of gene-body H3K36me3, with residual signal shifted towards promoters. In FANTOM6 CAGE, DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown activated the p53 pathway and triggered differential promoter usage in genes enriched for p53 and apoptotic regulators. Consistently, genes that gained gene-body H3K36me3 upon knockdown were enriched for apoptosis-related pathways. In line with high expression of DNAAF3-AS1 in testis, analysis based on the adult human testis single-cell atlas suggests that DNAAF3-AS1 may contribute to promoter-level H3K36me3 regulation during late spermatogenesis. Together, these results identify DNAAF3-AS1 as a chromatin-associated lncRNA that links H3K36me3 maintenance to p53 signalling.
